name: Basal Cell Carcinoma
description: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common form of skin cancer. It usually grows slowly over months or years on sun-exposed skin like the face, nose, and neck. It rarely spreads to other organs, but can damage local skin tissue if left untreated.
common_symptoms: A shiny, pearly, or translucent bump on the skin
Small visible red blood vessels across the bump
A sore or scab that bleeds, heals partly, and then returns
A pink growth with slightly raised rolled edges and a dent in the center
A flat, firm, pale or yellowish scar-like area with indistinct edges
causes: Damage to skin cell DNA from long-term sun exposure and UV rays
risk_factors: Light skin, blue or green eyes, or red/blond hair
Many years of outdoor work or intense sun exposure
first_aid: Do not scratch, peel, or pick at scabby bumps
Keep the skin area clean with mild soap and water
Shield the area from direct sun using a wide-brimmed hat
Schedule an evaluation with a doctor or dermatologist
precautions: Wear sunscreen with SPF 30+ every day on your face and neck
Wear wide-brimmed hats and sunglasses outside
Stay in the shade during midday sun (10 AM to 4 PM)
Watch for sores that fail to heal after 3 to 4 weeks
home_care: Gently wash the area with mild cleanser and pat dry
Do not put aggressive ointments or acids on the sore
do_not: DO NOT pick at crusty or pearly bumps repeatedly
DO NOT use over-the-counter wart removers on facial sores
DO NOT ignore a sore that repeatedly bleeds and fails to heal
red_flags: A persistent sore that fails to heal after 4 weeks
A growth located close to the eye, eyelid, nose, or ear
when_to_see_doctor: See a doctor or dermatologist if you notice a shiny bump, a non-healing scab, or a sore that repeatedly bleeds over 3 to 4 weeks.
prevention: Use broad-spectrum sunscreen daily on the face and neck
Wear hats and protective clothing in direct sun
